projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Glen R. Lindstrom was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran Glen R. Lindstrom. Mr. Lindstrom served with the U.S. Army 125th AAA gun battalion. he served in the European theater. I'm Tom Swope, and we recorded this at Mr. Lindstrom's home in Mentor, Ohio, on August 29, 2001. Glen's age at the time of this recording was 77. MR. LINDSTROM: Went into the army. I graduated from high school June 10th, sworn into the army on the 21st, and left on July 5th of '43. From there went to Columbus, Fort Hayes. And from there we went -- train to California. And on the way out, going by Benjamin Harrison -- I think it's Benjamin Harrison -- Indiana, we picked up a couple of trooploads of them too, and took them with us. And it was so nice, everybody thought we were going into the Air Corps. We pulled on the railroad track. On this side was the air force; on the other side was the anti-air force. And we ended up in the anti-air force.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And what would be the anti-air force?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: What would be the anti-air force? 125th Antiaircraft --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You weren't going to be flying planes; you were going to be shooting them down.

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Right. I can't remember the name of that town. The air force. Anyway, that's what we did. Then we trained there for a while. Then out to Camp Irwin, which is out in the desert, training center. And back. And then in February of '45 --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: '44, you mean?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: No -- yeah, '44. We went to troop training and ended up in Camp Edwards, Massachusetts, and then Miles Standish. And was that fun, because I knew a fellow that was in the -- a balloon pilot. And Bob said, "When you get out on the seas, you work your way up on the flying bridge, and when I come over, you wave to me. And when I wave to you, I'll take off." And that's exactly what he did. And of course, all the guys were along the rail. They were all waving. So he went by and saw me, I waved, and he took off. Three days out to sea was the last time I saw him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What happened to him?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: He went back to Massachusetts, and we went on over to England.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Go ahead and tell us again the places you went to when you got overseas.

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Where I went to?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where did you land in England?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: We landed at Liverpool and then we picked up our equipment at a little town called Blackshire Moor. Then we went down to Demchurch High in New Romney, down below Dover. And from there -- that was what they called Buzz Bomb Alley. And we were there for then until September. We went over there and we landed at Omaha. It was secure, but not -- they strafed it a couple of times while we were on the way in. We had a lot of fun on the way in. One Jeep pulled off the end of the ramp, got lost in the surf. so they had a big bulldozer come in and pull him out. Lots of fun. Then we were told to stay put, "You're going to be the antiaircraft protection for Shorebird " So we got up there, and they said, "Winterize. You're going to stay here all winter." We couldn't see the war lasting that long, but we did. And just as we got everything about where we wanted it, march order. We headed for Holland. Went all the way across France. And that was something. You go across France, you go into Belgium, it's like going from night into day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How was that? How was it different?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Well, just the way the Belgian people were so glad to see the Americans, where the French were not exactly. They were mad at the Americans for bombing their own -- bombing their territory. So, anyway, we went up there. Ended up -- I think we were pretty near up to the same place we come back to later. It was at Rosenthal. And then we stayed up there. That was Buzz Bomb Alley over there. So we were told that we were part of the antiaircraft protection for Antwerp. And then along come December 19th. We got. march order and we went down near the Battle of the Bulge. And that's where we -- on the way into the Battle of the Bulge in Leage we lost one gun and 14 men, just like that. Buzz bomb landed in a. treeline next to the gun, and it just blew it up. It had 75 rounds of ammunition on her too, and that blew up too. So there was no chance for -- those guys. didn't have a snowball's hell in chance. And then of course the rest of us kept going. And then we got down almost to Leage and they set us up as antitank guns because a ?9-A? could depress 2 degrees below zero. And we were able -- if we had to, we would have been able to shoot them. We didn't have to. That was the worst we had, was 14 men at one time. Out of the whole war, we lost a total of 18 men to combat, out of 700 men. Phenomenal.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have much luck shooting down any of the buzz bombs?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Oh, yes. We have -- I don't have with me, but we have papers that give us credit for shooting down 750 of them. Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is there any trick to shooting down a buzz bomb?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah. Hit them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Aim and hit?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah. And they're just that way. But then after the Battle of the Bulge, we went back up to Holland, because they were still shooting buzz bombs at Antwerp. And we were part of the antiaircraft protection for Antwerp. And we didn't know it then, but we were invited back in '94 for the 50th anniversary of the liberation of Antwerp, September 4th.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So what is the Antwerp X?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: That's what we were. Unattached, unassigned Antwerp X. We were known as "Antwerp X." That's what I told you before, we were unattached, unassigned. And that's how we got our mail, "Antwerp X." That's why I have on my license plate "125 AAA X." I wanted just 125, but one of the fellows living down in southern Ohio had it, so I couldn't get it. And I said, "What can I have, another letter?" Said, "Well, we used to be Antwerp X, so why not take 'X'?" So I did. So --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: All right. Continue. Where were we? Leage?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah. We moved back after that. We moved back up to Holland. And needless to say, the war sort of petered out then. And we were glad. And we made -- I don't have the book with me right this minute, but -- Ray happened to borrow it. and, you know, I'm supposed to pick it up tomorrow. Anyway, it's a history of my outfit from the time it was formed in California to the end of the war. And it was written by five different men writing the same story, so you get five different perspectives. Ray said it was very, very good. He just wished somebody in his outfit had done the same thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your job with the battery?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: I was battery aid man.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Battery aid man?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you do then?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Well, when they got a splinter in their little finger, I took it out. And if they got hurt, I took them off -- took care of them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So like a medic?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Each battery had one?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yes. Headquarters had a couple more than we did, because that's Headquarters, and the medics were simultaneous, it seemed. But each battery had at least one and sometimes two aid men, and that's where I was at. I used to live with the communications section, because our medical officer said he didn't give a damn what we did or when we did it, except when somebody wants you, needs you, he said "You better be Johnny on the spot." So that's why -- the communications section would have the complete -- knew where we were. That's it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any particularly tough times that you had to help with, a wounded situation that you had to deal with?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Well, yes. Just after Battle of the Bulge. a place called Tongras River. Moved back -- first place we went back to. Sergeant Shuldi was a radar operator. He was sitting at the radar, tracking a plane that was right around there. So this plane shot, and a 20-millimeter cannon shell went through the side of the radar, hit him on the right side and went right through him and come out the left side. And being a battery aid man, I had to take care of him. And there was no way to take care of him. He was dead the minute it hit him. So those kind of things aren't pleasant to remember.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you continue to move into Germany then after that?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: No. We went up into Holland, and that's where we stayed until we come -- from there, we got sent down to France. They started sending us down to the cigarette camps for preparation to go home. We were at Lucky Strike for a while and then we were at Phillip Morris. And then -- that's what they were, cigarette camps. And we had to stay there for a while until your number come up. We had 85, and we were in line to go home. so we did eventually, although I went home with the 75th Division because they wanted to put me -- they wanted me -- an infantryman in the army. And they also wanted to send me to Europe -- I mean, to the Philippines or wherever it was. I happened to have a medical MOS number, and without somebody pretty high up changing your MOS number, it's a pretty hard thing to do. So I didn't have to go. Got home February 20, 1946.

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were oversea in Europe that whole time?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember VE Day?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah. That was September 9th.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No. VE day.

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Oh. VE?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It would have been first part of May.

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Oh, May 9th. We, yeah, had quite a celebration. When you said "VE" I was thinking VJ. That was in September. It was in May, and of course everybody was happy to see that happen.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything you did in particular to celebrate?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Just happy?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How about VJ Day?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Same thing. We knew we didn't have to go there, and I was happy. Happiness, so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were still over there in Europe when they dropped the first atomic bomb?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction among the guys?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Unbelievable. You couldn't believe it, that someone could -- they said it destroyed so many thousands of people and everything else. Pretty hard to believe that. But now as time passes, you can understand how it happened. One big boom. And they wondered how on earth the guy created it, an atomic bomb.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have any memories of the day FDR died?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: April something -- '45.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Mm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: I remember it was quite surprising. everybody wasn't particularly happy. It was sort of a muted excitement. But it wasn't -- there wasn't any grand celebration.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you sad about -- was there a lot of sadness, or was it just another guy that died during the war?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: No. More so than that, because he was Commander-in-Chief. It wasn't a matter of just anybody dying. It was a matter of -- quite a difference. So --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of buddies over there, doing things with buddies?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah. We still have them. Since we came home, our outfit has had a reunion every year since 1947. And most of the time it's been in Columbus, because the fellows from Indiana, Kentucky, West Virginia, and Ohio congregate closer to Columbus than anything else, so we have our reunion in Columbus. We had one this year. Every year. There was 25 of us that got these this year.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Nice. So that's your --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The symbol for your company?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah. Well, now, what that -- that's Felix the Cat, and he's shooting a slingshot. And Felix -- that was the symbol, shooting down the buzz bombs. the symbol. We had a lot of fun that way. We had -- I wish that book was here right now. I know you would enjoy it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you don't remember any particular things about what you might have done with buddies for entertainment or anything like that to relieve the tension?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Well, really, our outfit was such that we didn't have to worry about tension. We weren't hard-pressed for anything like that. We had a very good outfit. And when you have an outfit like ours, it's not hard to get along with everybody. We didn't have any trouble, guys fighting or anything else. Everybody was happy. And the more we looked forward to going home, the happier we were. So we come home like February. I said February 20th in '46.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get much entertainment over there? U.S.O. shows? Anything like that?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: No. We were -- like, we were separated from everybody, because we were Antwerp X. They didn't know anything about us. The only thing we had was movies, and we had 35-millimeter brand-new cineplex projectors with a carbon arc. And I know, because I was the operator. I had a motion picture operator's license when I was in the service, so I got to show them at the cigarette camps. And we had a screen -- I don't know -- a great big tent, and show them up on the screen. Lots of fun.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you didn't see any --

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- big names?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Bob Hope or anybody like that? No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Bob didn't show up?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How about letters from home? Do you have any memories of mail call?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Well, after they found out where Antwerp X was, we used to get them. One thing I remember when I was -- we were up in Holland, it was so muddy and wet, I wrote home to my mother, "Send me my boots." I had knee boots. And she put them -- what she did, she rolled each one of them up separately, one in one package and one in the other. And she had to show them a letter saying that I wanted them. And I got them. And I wore them up there until I ran out of them one time. Got so mad at them, I quit wearing them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Who did she have to explain that to?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Post office.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Post Office?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They didn't understand why she would be sending something like that to a soldier?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah. Unless you had a request for it, they wouldn't send it. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Because they probably didn't have room to send a lot of stuff, or what?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Well, you had to have a request for it. I don't know. I wasn't there, except I knew Mother had to have it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What would be your most vivid memory of that experience over there? Anything come to mind?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Well, just after pulling back out of the Battle of the Bulge, and when Sergeant Shuldi got killed and I had to take care of him. By the way, when we went over there in '94, we went and visited a couple of cemeteries. We went around and I saw the fellows from -- what's the name of the outfit -- that got killed. That whole group with the machine gun? We saw the monument for that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: At Malmedy?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah. And then we saw all that. And saw other -- and out of all that things, we only found five graves that were the fellows -- where they were buried. And I remember some of them never even got buried, because the way it exploded I think they maybe got just blown to bits. Nothing there to bury. So that's -- those are the kind of things you like to forget about.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any trouble adjusting when you got back home?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Didn't have to deal with any dreams or nightmares? That sort of thing?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: I had intended to be a mortician, because that's where I was working before I went in. I went down to the funeral home, walked in, got one mental picture of all the fellows I had seen killed and told Don, I said, "That's it. Good-bye." Changed your mind.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you had seen enought of that, huh?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah. When we first went in, the first train ride we had was from Ohio through Indiana and clear out to California. One long trip. And it seemed it took forever to get there. But that's where we ended up. Then out to Camp Irwin, the desert training center for Camp Hahn, which was just outside Riverside. And now Camp Hahn is now a national cemetery, Riverside National Cemetery, where Camp Hahn used to be. And we have a plaque on the wall out there. I don't know whether I have got a picture of it or not. But we have a picture of it around someplace.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have to train on a gun?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Because you knew you were going to be a medic from the beginning?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: I didn't, no. No, I didn't.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No basic training in case you --

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: No, I didn't have to. But I had fun with the fellows. Because I didn't have to do anything, they let me -- just for the fun of it, when they were practicing they let me fire. And I held on to the -- you squeeze it, and they didn't tell me I wasn't supposed to hang on to it until I was ready to squeeze it. I shoved it home, and I had my hand on it and, boom, she's coming back, firing by me. We had one fellow, I can't remember his name, he used to scrape his belly all the time when the breach come by. Nothing serious or anything, but just the idea it would come sliding by, because he never did anything but hold on to the trigger, where I just happened to have ahold of it when I shoved it home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Like standing too close to a --

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- and got hurt when it came back?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Don't they tell them where to stand?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Well, let's put it this way: They don't tell you a lot of things, but you learn real quick. You got the story I told you about the blimp coming over, three days out to sea. I told you I was up on the -- Bob said, "Work your way up to the flying bridge, get out on the end of it so I can see you." When he could see me, I waved, he waved back, and he took off. The poor guys down on the deck couldn't figure out "What the heck is he doing?"

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They thought you had control?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, was that blimp on submarine duty?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah. Out of Weymouth, Massachusetts, because that's where Bob was. We were in Boston, Camp Edwards, and having known him all my life. He happened to be a balloon pilot, that's all.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I guess that wouldn't be too hard.

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: No. Balloons, they are fun to fly in.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did he tell you, could they see submarines pretty easily?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Oh, yeah. If you're looking down through the water --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: If the water is clear enough --

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: It depends. No, not clear enough. The shimmer on the water is harder to see through than anything else. as soon as you get to a spot where you can see through the water -- see through the shim, with all the dancing pieces, when you can see through that, then you can see down real good. I don't know whether they ever had to bomb any that I know of. But that was what the purpose was. I heard one time that they carried a bomb.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: On the blimp?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That would be kind of a hard thing to do, though, wouldn't it?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: As long as -- well, I guess the blimps and the submarine move at about the same rate?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Oh, yeah. And go over and release it and drop it right down. Just be high enough so that it don't -- the water don't get you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: A depth charge?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah -- not a depth charge. A regular bomb.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: An actual bomb?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah. I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were they bombing on the surface?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: No. Down below. So they go through and then it would blow up. I guess hitting the water with that force would set the bomb off just as well as anything else.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That's interesting. I wonder if a blimp ever got one. It seems like it would be a tough thing to do.

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: They treated -- the Belgians treated you like royalty. And we were invited by the King and Queen, and we had dinner in City Hall. I mean, you know you're welcome.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But the French --

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Didn't they understand that we had to bomb France? There was not much choice?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: I don't know. But even on VE Day -- no. It wasn't that. It was a celebration. Fiftieth anniversary of it, Peter Jennings was over there. And at that time, there were people who were still ticked off at the United States for bombing France. But when we come in across over Omaha, we saw St. Lo, and St. Lo was nothing but one chimney standing when we saw it. It had been sort of wiped out. But we didn't have anything to do with it; we were just passing through, so we didn't fire on anything. We only fired at buzz bombs. I shouldn't say the only thing. We fired one time at a flight of B17s that were coming back. They come in right on the buzz bomb course and they wouldn't identify themselves on the IFF. Fired two shots, and they dove at us. And when they dove at us they could see it was B17s, and they ceased fire. Nobody got shot down, but they knew that we were there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I don't think we got the story on tape about the B17 that went down and the crewman that was running away. Tell that again.

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: You mean -- oh, during the Battle of the Bulge, a B17 got shot down, and he jumped out, parachute. And when he come down, he was running away from us. And we couldn't stop him. And needless to say, when he heard us cussing away, Americans doing the cussing, he knew he was not in German territory.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He was running toward the German lines?

sp.speaker: Glen R. Lindstrom
sp.p: Yeah. But when he heard that, he -- yes. Someplace, I don't know where it is right now, I think I still have a piece of that shroud cord, you know, that holds the parachute up. Someplace I think I still have it.
